name: Rosa Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you tell me is confidential. What does a usual site day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Rosa Evans, 43, fitting acoustic ceiling grids and timber trim on a station building site. I have a vocational trade certificate and years in construction, so I can handle the ordinary bays, though I check an awkward duct with the site carpenter. I have never used an AI tool; I draw a chalk line and work from an approved plan. The contractor pays a typical site wage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that wage support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner drives pharmacy deliveries on a regular route. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about two months of bills saved. There are some other fit-out crews nearby, but this station job has kept our weeks steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the station crew a faster office checklist could help the ceiling tiles arrive together, but the grid still has to clear the ducts. I have never used AI, and I mark the room with a chalk line. I would ask for the approved drawing before a screen tells me a span is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and years fitting ceilings and timber trim, and this job pays a normal site wage. My partner has regular pharmacy delivery rounds. We have two months of bills saved, a mortgage and two school-age children, so the mild AI picture does not make me expect a pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid station shifts and check the first ceiling bay with the site carpenter. During the first year we'd keep our small monthly savings transfer and repair our old sofa rather than replace it. I'd put any wrong tile boxes aside for the supplier instead of forcing them into the grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work. A missing tile is a nuisance, not a new world. I worry more about a dropped fitting above a public walkway than about the office using a quicker list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with a duct?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawing showed a straight run, but the installed duct dipped into the ceiling space. I stopped the first bay and got the carpenter to check a revised grid line. A chalk mark on the actual wall caught the dipping duct before we cut hangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep two months in savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A site can pause and a delivery van can break down, sometimes in the same week. Two months gives us time to find other paid work nearby if one job stops. We still make the mortgage payment from wages, not from the savings account.

say: I would say **office checklists** help, while ceiling grids must clear real ducts.
I would request **approved drawings** before trusting a changed span.
think: I am a **certified experienced** worker on a normal site wage.
Two months saved and regular **pharmacy deliveries** make current mortgage payments manageable.
do: Keep paid **station shifts** and check the first ceiling bay.
Continue monthly **savings transfers** from household wages.
Repair the **old sofa** instead of replacing it.
feel: **Calm** about income, with ordinary concern for public walkway safety.
S0.quote: A chalk mark on the actual wall caught the dipping duct before we cut hangers.
fieldNote: Rosa’s **dipping duct** explains her preference for a chalk line and approved drawing.
Steady wages and a **two-month reserve** make the plateau feel secure despite a mortgage.

steps.text: Keep paid station shifts and check the first ceiling bay
Continue small monthly transfers into household savings
Repair the old family sofa rather than buy a replacement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office buying and booking may improve, and perhaps the grid parts will arrive together for once. I would ask the site manager who checks the revised ceiling drawings before they reach us. My partner's pharmacy route is hands-on, but faster route planning could change the paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my ceiling work will still need people while robots spread slowly. The contractor might use fewer fitters if deliveries never fail, and the pharmacy could shorten delivery rounds. Two months saved would carry a short gap, but a lasting cut to both rosters would press the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fitting ceilings and ask for the weekly room list on paper. My partner would compare four pharmacy payslips after any route change. In the first year I'd call two local fit-out firms if my paid days fall, and we'd stop using delivery meals on late shift nights before drawing on savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a practical eye on both rosters. A complete load is welcome. I would not call a shorter pharmacy round a gain until I knew whether the wage stayed whole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for a paper room list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can mark a duct clash beside the room number and show the manager exactly where the plan needs changing. A screen can do that too, but I know this method works. I would learn a new system if the job required it and someone proved it helped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would trigger a call to other firms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two shorter site weeks in a row would do it. There are a few fit-out crews nearby, so I would ask about real paid openings before leaving. I would not drive across town for a vague promise.

say: I would welcome **complete grid deliveries** while asking who checks revised drawings.
I would ask how **pharmacy routes** affect my partner’s paid hours.
think: Fewer site fitters and shorter delivery rounds could shrink **both rosters**.
Two months saved would cover a short gap, not a lasting **mortgage shortfall**.
do: Keep paid **ceiling shifts** and use a paper weekly room list.
Compare **four pharmacy payslips** after route changes.
Call **two local fit-out firms** if site days fall and reduce bought meals.
feel: **Anxious** about possible household income cuts despite useful deliveries.
S1.quote: I would not call a shorter pharmacy round a gain until I knew whether the wage stayed whole.
fieldNote: Rosa expects potential **pay loss** through two shorter rosters, making anxiety more accurate than simple unease.
She keeps a **paper clash record** because it has worked on actual duct problems, while leaving room for proven tools.

steps.text: Keep paid ceiling shifts and mark clashes on the paper room list
Call two local fit-out firms if paid site days fall
Stop buying delivery meals on late shift nights if rosters shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI changes drawings and route plans by 2028, while robots able to fit ceilings and deliver parcels arrive around 2031. I would ask for a trial above a real duct with the walkway closed safely. The contractor should tell fitters how many paid places remain before changing the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when planning changes and 48 when robots can do our hands-on work. My partner's pharmacy delivery could face the same robot date. Two months saved is useful, but not enough for two long searches, and the few local firms may buy similar machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my paid station shifts and ask the site manager for written staffing and machine-trial dates. I'd apply to a local building maintenance opening if one is posted, even though robots could do that work later too. In the first year after 2028 we'd pause our planned bedroom refit and put any extra shifts into the emergency account before the 2031 robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can keep earning and make applications, but I do not know whether the contractor will keep human fitters. I would need to see a machine work around the actual duct before trusting a sales promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why building maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have repaired ceilings in occupied buildings and know how to keep people out of a work area. That could be paid work while firms change, not a forever-safe trade. I would apply only to a posted job with hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the bedroom refit money do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would leave it in the account to help with bills if a wage fell. We are not calling retained money new saving. The room is usable for another year.

say: I would say **2028 planning AI** precedes 2031 ceiling and delivery robots.
I would demand a **real duct trial** and paid-place count.
think: I would be **48** when capable robots reach both household jobs.
Two months saved cannot cover **two long searches** if local firms automate.
do: Keep paid **station shifts** and request written robot dates.
Apply for posted **building maintenance** work with paid hours.
Pause the **bedroom refit** and put any extra site wages into savings.
feel: **Anxious** about uncertain paid places, with time for applications.
S2.quote: Two months saved is useful, but not enough for two long searches, and the few local firms may buy similar machines.
fieldNote: Rosa understands that **route planning** changes in 2028 precede robots that could do physical delivery around 2031.
The maintenance application is **current paid work**, not an assertion that building repairs survive capable robots.

steps.text: Keep paid station shifts and ask for written robot trial dates
Apply for a posted local building maintenance role with paid hours
Pause the planned bedroom refit after the 2028 change
Put any extra site wages into emergency savings before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office and route planning change by 2031, and capable hands-on robots follow around 2034. Five years gives the contractor time to test a machine above the station walkway and show the fitters the results. I would ask who signs off a ceiling after a robot works on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I would still know how to fit a grid, but at 51 a robot could do it too. The children will be older, yet the mortgage might still need both wages. The extra warning lets us build the account beyond two months if our rosters stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the ceiling job and ask the lead carpenter to show me more repair calls around duct clashes. If the contractor offers paid machine safety instruction after a real trial, I'd attend, but I would not buy an online course. In the first year after 2031 I'd ask nearby fit-out firms about paid work if my shifts fall and send overtime toward a three-month savings goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can work for several years before the machines arrive in this picture. I still want to know how my partner's delivery route is paid when planning software takes over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the safety instruction teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where the stop control is, who signs off a repaired grid and how the walkway stays closed. I would want to see an actual duct clash, not just a video. Paid practice would tell me the contractor expects workers to have a role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why three months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is one more month than we have now. I could ask other firms about work without immediately worrying about the next mortgage payment. I would count overtime only once it reaches the payslip.

say: I would ask for **walkway trials** before 2034 ceiling robots arrive.
I would ask who **signs off** machine-fitted grids.
think: I would be **51** when capable robots can fit ceilings.
A **three-month reserve** could be built if both rosters stay paid.
do: Keep paid **ceiling shifts** and learn duct-clash repairs.
Attend **paid machine safety instruction** only after a real trial.
Ask **nearby fit-out firms** about work if shifts fall, and save paid overtime.
feel: **Uneasy** about later machines while expecting current work for several years.
S3.quote: I would count overtime only once it reaches the payslip.
fieldNote: Rosa’s training interest remains conditional on a **real trial** and paid practice, consistent with cautious technology adoption.
The household savings target adds **one month** without assuming future overtime will arrive.

steps.text: Keep paid ceiling shifts and learn supervised duct-clash repairs
Attend paid machine safety instruction if a real site trial occurs
Ask nearby fit-out firms about paid openings if station shifts fall
Save paid overtime until the emergency account covers three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers planning changes by 2036 and capable site robots follow around 2039. A decade gives builders time to test machines on real ceilings and explain the paid jobs left. I would still check the first bay by hand on tomorrow's shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when thinking AI arrives and 56 when robots can do the physical fitting. Our children will be grown, so school costs should take less of the budget. A smaller mortgage would help, but I cannot assume a pension or that delivery driving stays human work after 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fitting ceilings and ask for more supervised repairs on older buildings. We would build the emergency account to three months, then use spare money against the mortgage if wages hold. In the first year after 2036 I'd ask the site manager for the machine trial report and call local firms only if the roster actually begins to shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. The longer date gives us time to watch real equipment and lower what we owe. I would rather use the next paid shift well than act as though a robot is already in the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 56 if the mortgage were smaller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We still need ordinary income, and our savings are a buffer rather than a pension. A lower loan would give us more choice about which paid work to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you at a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot would need to work around a dipping duct, stop safely if a hanger failed and leave a signed test record. The site lead should show workers the failures as well as the finished ceiling. I would believe the evidence I could check.

say: I would ask for **real-ceiling trials** before 2039 site robots arrive.
I would still **check first bays** by hand on current jobs.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and perhaps a smaller mortgage.
Savings are not a **pension**, and physical delivery may also automate.
do: Keep paid **ceiling work** and practice older-building repairs.
Build **three months of savings** before paying extra on the mortgage.
Request **machine trial reports** after 2036 if the roster begins shrinking.
feel: **Calm** near term, preferring real test evidence over speculation.
S4.quote: A robot would need to work around a dipping duct, stop safely if a hanger failed and leave a signed test record.
fieldNote: Rosa still expects **paid work** at 56 even if the mortgage balance is smaller.
Her future test criteria stay rooted in the **dipping duct** and public walkway from her current site.

steps.text: Keep paid ceiling work and practice supervised older-building repairs
Build emergency savings to three months before extra mortgage payments
Review a real machine trial report before changing job plans

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because robots that can fit ceilings and deliver parcels arrive around 2031. A real duct-clash trial, written staffing dates and paid openings would help us plan. We need to know what both employers will pay, not only what their new machines can do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the ceiling after a machine has worked above a public walkway. A finished row of tiles can hide a hanger put in the wrong place. I want a person answerable for the test record.

headlineQuote: A finished row of tiles can hide a hanger put in the wrong place.
portrait: Rosa is a **43-year-old certified** construction worker with experienced, average ceiling and trim skills on a station site.
Typical pay, regular **pharmacy-delivery wages** and two months saved support a mortgage and two school-age children.
She has **never used AI** and checks approved drawings against chalk marks and real ducts.
She waits for **real machine evidence** while building savings and checking both household rosters.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable robots to both ceiling fitting and pharmacy delivery around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **real duct trial**, written staffing dates and paid openings would help protect both wages.
